 Amir Jangoo continues to impress with the ­willow, the Trinidad and Tobago wicket-keeper-batter ­notching his second Test match century on day two of the second Test between West Indies and Bangladesh, in ­Sylhet.
 The Sylhet Test is only Jangoo’s seventh, but he has ­already made a name for himself in the cricketing world and has sealed his place in the West Indies middle-order. So, all things being equal, you can look forward to seeing the St James batter in full flight at Test venues around the globe for many years to come.
 Jangoo, though, does not play Test cricket only. He has played 12 One Day Internationals for the regional team, scoring two centuries, including an unbeaten 104 against Bangladesh on debut in December 2024. The second ton, 114, was scored just five weeks ago in India. An impressive average of 58.37 is a clear indicator of the batter’s quality. Add seven T20Is to his list of international appearances.
 Jangoo is an all-format player who can make the necessary adjustments to his game. Just hand him a bat, point him to a pitch, and he’ll do the rest.
 The purists, though, will tell you that Test cricket is THE true test. So far, Jangoo is passing with flying colours. He made his five-day cricket debut in Multan, Pakistan, in January 2025. It was anything but memorable, Jangoo making a duck in his very first Test knock. He bounced back in the West Indies second innings with 30.
 Jangoo was made to wait a long time for a second opportunity to impress while wearing whites and the maroon cap. Exactly 17 months after the Multan debut, Jangoo was selected in the final West Indies eleven for the first Test against Sri Lanka at the Sir Vivian Richards Stadium, in Antigua. The rest is history.
 The June 2026 West Indies/Sri Lanka Test produced a special performance: a splendid knock of 233 from the bat of Amir Anthony Jangoo. In just his second Test and third innings at the highest level, not only did he get to 100, he turned his maiden ton into a double century, announcing his arrival to the world.
 What was it that transformed Jangoo into a Test match run machine? Perhaps, playing at the Viv Richards Ground ­inspired him to do something the Master Blaster himself would be proud of. Or maybe, 17 months of waiting had produced an inward hunger and desperate desire to not be overlooked by the selectors ever again.
 Whatever it was, a star was born and West Indies romped to a massive innings and 217-run victory.
 A three-ball duck in the first Test against Bangladesh, last week, showed Jangoo’s human side. Seems as though that scoreless knock also brought out the beast in the left-hander, his 133 in the ongoing Sylhet Test putting West Indies in pole position.
 Jangoo, the only player in history to have turned his first three first-class centuries into double tons, is a special talent. He’s the real deal.
